subject_line: Archie the alpaca and the festival in The Brilliant & Forever
email_body:
Dear Kevin,

The Brilliant & Forever stayed with me for its version of Lewis where humans and alpacas coexist, and for three friends, one of them Archie the alpaca, competing at the island's literary festival. It manages to be a satire on what we value in culture while also being about friendship and belonging. I'd like to ask how Archie first arrived on the page, and how you kept the comedy and the seriousness in balance.

subject_line: The barrel on the Killybegs shore in The Boy from the Sea
email_body:
Dear Garrett,

The Boy from the Sea opens so memorably, with a newborn in a barrel washing up at Killybegs in 1973 and Ambrose Bonnar taking the child into his family, all told by an unnamed narrator who acts as the town's chronicler. I'd be interested to ask why you chose that collective, insider voice, and how writing about a real place compared with your nonfiction in The Rule of the Land.

subject_line: The four girls of summer 1988 in We Play Here
email_body:
Dear Dawn,

We Play Here has stayed with me for its four girls in Protestant North Belfast in the summer of 1988, caught between primary school and high school, each telling her part as a poem-story. I'd love to ask why the verse novel form felt right for that summer, and how you decided which of the four friends should carry each part of it.

subject_line: Your grandfather and Beckett in Jott
email_body:
Dear Sam,

Jott caught my attention for the way it draws on the 1930s friendship between your grandfather and Samuel Beckett, working from real letters between the two men into a novel about friendship, madness and modernism. I'd be interested to ask how you balanced the documentary record against invention, and whether writing so close to family history changed how you approached it compared with Communion Town.

subject_line: One solstice day with the Avens family
email_body:
Dear Elizabeth,

An Archive of Happiness held me with its frame: a single solstice day in the Scottish Highlands, as the fractured Avens family gathers for their annual get-together. I'd be interested to ask what keeping the novel to one day allowed you to do with a family's history, and how coming to Scotland from Chicago shapes the way you write the Highland landscape.

subject_line: Charity shops and queer art in You Name It
email_body:
Dear Colin,

You Name It caught my attention for how widely it ranges, from queer art and ekphrasis to pop culture, grief and charity shops, all within one collection. I'd like to ask how those very different subjects find their way into the same book, and how editing and introducing centenary volumes for Joan Eardley and Edwin Morgan has fed back into your own poems.

subject_line: Writing The Lighthouse Witches as CJ Cooke
email_body:
Dear Carolyn,

The Lighthouse Witches, nominated for both an Edgar and an ITW Thriller Award, sits within a run of gothic novels you have written as CJ Cooke, alongside The Nesting and The Book of Witching. I'd be interested to ask what drew you to the gothic as a form, and how publishing fiction under a different name from your poetry and academic work has changed how you think about each.
